summary: An excerpt from a fiction work ("Book 4 — part 36") following Anda and her leader Lucy, who run paid in-game missions in a online game on Fahrenheit Island. Anda now has real cash income, and the pair take a close-to-home mission, ambushing sniper lookouts with BFGs and scrying spells. Anda questions why anyone pays so much for these jobs, and Lucy dismisses the worry with a money-as-relative-value argument involving frappuccinos and child support.
one_line: Anda and Lucy take a paid in-game mission on Fahrenheit Island and debate why the money is so good.
key_facts: Anda now has pocket-money for the first time in her life, which she can spend outside the 500 meter sugar-free zone around her school.
Anda is described as the richest kid she knows and is suddenly everybody's best pal, with handfuls of Curly that she can selectively distribute to schoolmates.
Lucy's voice in Anda's ear is described as a constant companion, and the two run missions into the wee hours of the night.
The Fahrenheit armorers are non-player-characters who have learned to recognise Anda and keep the Clan's BFGs oiled and ready for her.
Lucy says "Money talks and bullshit walks" and prefers cash to gold and experience to experience points.
Anda uses a scrying spell to spot the first round of sniper/lookouts, and Lucy fires at the hilltops flanking the roadway before they reach bow range.
Anda asks Lucy, whom she calls Sarge, why anyone would pay cash for these missions, and Lucy asks whether anyone is asking Anda to cyber some old pervert.
Lucy suggests the paying clients may be two rich gamers who pay their butlers to craft for them all day, one fucking with the other.
Lucy states that most of the world lives on about a dollar a day and that she spends five dollars every day on a frappuccino, sometimes two.
Lucy says her dad sends her mom three thousand a month in child-support, which is about a hundred bucks a day.
Lucy calculates that if a day's money in the game is worth a hundred, her frappuccino is worth about five hundred dollars and she buys two or three every day.
Lucy's dad loved an old TV show and makes the "Hey, Lucy!" joke every visitation day.
